content: In probability and statistics, a Bernoulli process is a discrete-time stochastic process that consists of a sequence of independent random variables, each of which can take on one of two possible values. These values are often referred to as success and failure, and are typically represented numerically as 1 and 0, respectively. Each random variable in the sequence is called a Bernoulli variable, and the probability of success (i.e., the variable taking the value 1) is denoted by ( p ), which remains constant across all trials. A Bernoulli process can be thought of as a sequence of independent and identically distributed Bernoulli trials. For example, it is analogous to repeatedly flipping a coin, where the coin may or may not be fair. The independence of the trials implies that the outcome of any given trial does not influence the outcomes of future trials. This property is often referred to as memorylessness. Consequently, at any point in time, the future trials form a Bernoulli process that is independent of the past, a property known as the fresh-start property. Random variables associated with a Bernoulli process include: The number of successes in the first ( n ) trials, which follows a binomial distribution. The number of trials required to achieve ( r ) successes, which follows a negative binomial distribution. The number of trials required to achieve a single success, which follows a geometric distribution (a special case of the negative binomial distribution). The problem of determining whether a coin is fair, based on a limited sample of Bernoulli trials, is a classic example of statistical inference in the context of a Bernoulli process. Formal Definition A Bernoulli process can be formally defined within the framework of probability spaces. Specifically, it is a probability space ( (Omega, Pr) ) along with a random variable ( X ) that takes values in the set ({0, 1}). For every ( omega in Omega ), the random variable ( X_i(omega) ) equals 1 with probability ( p ) and equals 0 with probability ( 1 p ). Bernoulli Sequence Given a Bernoulli process defined on a probability space ( (Omega, Pr) ), each ( omega in Omega ) corresponds to a sequence of integers known as the Bernoulli sequence. For instance, if ( omega ) represents a sequence of coin flips, the Bernoulli sequence is the list of integers indicating the trials where the coin landed heads. Almost all Bernoulli sequences are ergodic, meaning that their statistical properties are representative of the entire process. Bernoulli Map Since each trial in a Bernoulli process has one of two possible outcomes, a sequence of trials can be represented using the binary digits of a real number. When the probability ( p = 1/2 ), all possible distributions of outcomes are equally likely. In this case, the measure of the ( sigma )-algebra of the Bernoulli process is equivalent to the uniform measure on the unit interval. In other words, the real numbers are uniformly distributed on the interval ([0, 1]). The shift operator ( T ), which maps each random variable to the next one in the sequence, is described by the Bernoulli map (or the ( 2x mod 1 ) map). For a given sequence of measurements ( z ), the Bernoulli map essentially removes one digit from the binary expansion of ( z ). This map serves as an exactly solvable model of deterministic chaos. The transfer operator (or Frobenius-Perron operator) associated with the Bernoulli map is also solvable, with eigenvalues that are multiples of ( 1/2 ) and eigenfunctions that are Bernoulli polynomials. Generalizations The Bernoulli process can be generalized to scenarios with more than two possible outcomes. This generalization is referred to as the Bernoulli scheme.
